findings.problem: fs::read_to_string(path).unwrap() panics on I/O failure (missing file, permission denied, etc.)
findings.failure_mode: External/untrusted file path causes process abort instead of returning a typed error to the caller
findings.fix: Return Result<Vec<Record>, io::Error> (or a domain error enum) and propagate with ? operator

findings.failure_mode: Malformed CSV data (e.g. 'alpha,beta') aborts the process instead of returning a typed parse error
findings.fix: Use parts[1].parse::<u32>().map_err(|e| ParseError::InvalidValue { field: parts[0].clone(), reason: e.to_string() }) and propagate with ?

findings.problem: as u16 cast silently truncates u32 values above 65535
findings.failure_mode: A valid u32 like 70000 silently wraps to 4464, producing incorrect audit data with no indication of data loss
findings.fix: Use u16::try_from(parts[1].parse::<u32>()?).map_err(|_| RangeError::ValueTooLarge) or parse directly as u16 with parts[1].parse::<u16>().unwrap()...

findings.problem: parts[0] accesses index 0 of a Vec that could be empty if line is empty or has no commas
findings.failure_mode: Empty line or line with no comma causes index-out-of-bounds panic
findings.fix: Use split_once(',') and handle None, or check parts.len() before indexing

findings.problem: parts[1] accesses index 1 without checking length; line with single field (no comma) has Vec length 1
findings.failure_mode: Line with no comma (e.g. 'solo_line') panics on index 1 access before even reaching parse
findings.fix: Check parts.len() >= 2 or use split_once(',') which yields exactly 0 or 2 branches

findings.problem: println!() is a side-effecting I/O call inside what should be a pure parsing pipeline
findings.failure_mode: Hidden logging side effect makes the function non-deterministic, harder to test in isolation, and couples the parsing core to stdout. Violates functional core / imperative shell separation.
findings.fix: Remove println! from the core. If audit logging is needed, return a separate log/trace type from a shell function, or accept a writer callback in the shell layer

findings.problem: load_audits mixes file I/O (fs::read_to_string) with parsing logic in a single function
findings.failure_mode: Cannot unit-test the parsing logic without mocking the filesystem; pure parse behavior is not isolated from I/O failure modes
findings.fix: Split into (a) fn parse_records(lines: &[&str]) -> Result<Vec<Record>, ParseError> (pure core) and (b) fn load_audits(path: &str) -> Result<Vec<Record>, IoError> (shell that reads file and delegates to core)

findings.problem: Collects every split part into Vec<String> with owned clones instead of using split_once or borrowed slices
findings.failure_mode: Unnecessary heap allocations per line; for large audit files this compounds into significant memory pressure and GC pressure. The grammar expects exactly 2 fields but collects all of them into owned Strings.
findings.fix: Use line.split_once(',') to get (&str, &str) directly without allocation, then .trim() those borrowed slices

missing_evidence: no benchmark exists for file I/O throughput or parsing performance
no profiler data for allocation profiles under realistic audit file sizes
no second-ring command evidence (no cargo test, cargo clippy, or Miri runs)
no benchmark/profiler/allocation/command evidence per Holzman performance discipline
residual_risk: Static review only; no commands run. All 6 blocker findings are direct violation of zero-forbidden-constructs rules (unwrap, unchecked indexing, lossy cast, hidden I/O side effect). The function as-written will panic on any malformed input, missing file, or value outside u16 range. Functional core/shell boundary is violated with println! in the parsing loop.
